reference.source: ESC/AHA guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death; Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents in childhood or adolescence with syncope, seizures, or cardiac arrest triggered by exercise or intense emotion, in a structurally normal heart
The resting ECG is typically normal, so a high index of suspicion and provocative testing are essential
Exercise or catecholamine stress testing reproducibly elicits ventricular ectopy that progresses to bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia as heart rate rises
Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance through cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) variants; a rarer autosomal recessive form is caused by calsequestrin (CASQ2) variants
Beta-blockers, particularly non-selective agents such as nadolol, are the cornerstone of therapy and reduce arrhythmic events
Flecainide is a useful adjunct that suppresses calcium-driven ectopy, and left cardiac sympathetic denervation is an option for refractory disease
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is reserved for survivors of cardiac arrest or those with breakthrough events despite optimal medical therapy
Family cascade genetic screening and counselling are important because relatives may carry the variant while appearing clinically normal
reference.pathophysiology: CPVT arises from dysregulated calcium handling in cardiac myocytes. Variants in the ryanodine receptor (RYR2) or calsequestrin (CASQ2) genes destabilise the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel complex, so that during adrenergic stimulation calcium leaks into the cytosol during diastole. This calcium overload drives delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under the influence of circulating catecholamines generate the characteristic exercise- or emotion-induced bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia despite an anatomically normal heart. Sustained runs may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death.
additionalDifferentials: Digoxin toxicity causing bidirectional ventricular tachycardia
additionalInvestigations: Exercise treadmill or bicycle stress testing to provoke reproducible ectopy and bidirectional VT
Ambulatory (Holter) monitoring to capture exertional arrhythmia burden
12-lead resting ECG (usually normal, helps exclude QT prolongation and other channelopathies)
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to confirm structurally normal heart and exclude cardiomyopathy
Targeted genetic testing for RYR2 and CASQ2 variants
Cascade genetic and clinical screening of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Exertional or emotion-triggered syncope or seizure in a young person
Aborted cardiac arrest or documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Family history of sudden death, drowning, or unexplained syncope in youth
Recurrent arrhythmic events despite beta-blocker therapy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, adherence to beta-blockade with or without flecainide, and activity modification, arrhythmic events can be substantially reduced; however, untreated or poorly controlled CPVT carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from adolescence onward.
pitfalls: Dismissing exertional syncope as vasovagal because the resting ECG and echocardiogram are normal
Relying on a single resting ECG rather than provocative exercise testing to make the diagnosis
Under-dosing beta-blockade or accepting poor adherence, leaving breakthrough arrhythmia
Placing an ICD as sole therapy, since painful shocks can trigger an adrenergic surge and further arrhythmia
Overlooking the need to screen and counsel apparently healthy relatives
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Non-selective beta-blockade, particularly nadolol, as first-line therapy to blunt catecholamine-driven triggered activity
Add flecainide when beta-blockade alone incompletely suppresses exercise-induced ventricular ectopy
Strict avoidance of competitive or strenuous exercise and intensely emotional triggers
Left cardiac sympathetic denervation for arrhythmia refractory to combined drug therapy
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for survivors of cardiac arrest or breakthrough syncope, combined with drugs to limit shock storms
Serial exercise and ambulatory (Holter) testing to confirm arrhythmia suppression and titrate therapy
Genetic counselling with cascade RYR2/CASQ2 testing and clinical screening of first-degree relatives
Emergency preparedness with automated external defibrillator access and family cardiopulmonary resuscitation training
